item.title: The Power of Positive: The Neuroscience of Affirmation
item.description:
Positive Psychology

The Power of Positive: The Neuroscience of Affirmation

How language leaders use with themselves shapes how they think, respond and lead

Posted August 14, 2026

Key points
  • Your brain is always listening to you.
  • Temporary experiences should not become permanent identities.
  • A leader's internal dialogue eventually becomes the organizational climate.

Now that you have read the title, you might be thinking, “Oh no, not one of these feel-good articles.” And before you think I am advocating for participation trophies, artificial optimism, or the belief that everyone deserves first-place recognition, I am not. I actually believe struggle, difficulty, and failure build character. Somewhere I heard, “If every day is a sunny day, then what’s a sunny day?” There is wisdom in that question. We only recognize a sunny day because we have experienced rain, clouds, and storms.

In the same way, achievement only feels meaningful because we have known disappointment. Growth only occurs because we have struggled. And success is only fully appreciated when we have encountered some setbacks along the way. Without contrast, our victories become ordinary, and our blessings become invisible.

The same principle applies to leadership. Great leaders are not made during periods of comfort. Great leaders are tested and tried along the journey.

True leadership requires resilience. It requires discomfort. Positive psychology does not reject hardship. In many ways, it assumes hardship is inevitable. What positive psychology and neuroscience suggest is that the way leaders speak to themselves during hardship matters far more than many realize.

Remember this: Your brain is always listening to you. And the language you repeatedly use with yourself can shape your stress response and emotional regulation. That’s not motivational speaking. That is neuroscience.

At a recent strengths-based leadership workshop, an assistant principal raised his hand during a discussion about leadership identity and burnout. Looking defeated, he said, “Honestly, I suck at being an assistant principal.”

The room shifted. A few people nodded. Maybe they were recognizing some version of that thought in themselves.

I responded, “The first thing I want you to do is adjust your language to describe the fact that you are struggling right now. There is a difference between saying, ‘I am struggling with part of my job,’ and saying, ‘I suck at it.’ One describes a challenge. The other is what you are speaking into existence.”

Then I asked him a few questions.

“Has a student trusted you this year?” Yes.

“Has a teacher thanked you?” Yes.

“Have you handled a difficult situation better than you would have two years ago?” He laughed. “Definitely.”

“Then that’s evidence of growth, not failure.”

The room was suddenly full of “ohs” and “ahhs.” I am certain that people recognized themselves in the exchange.

Nothing about his job had changed. His workload was going to be the same. The stress was still there. What changed was the story he was telling himself about it. After our exchange, he was no longer seeing himself through the lens of his struggle. He understood it as a developmental moment. That distinction matters neurologically and psychologically.

Neuroscience and psychology are catching up with an idea found in Eastern religions and philosophies for millennia: As you think, so you are. Research on positive thinking and self-talk suggests that optimistic thought patterns are associated with lower stress levels, improved coping skills, stronger psychological well-being, and better physical health outcomes.1

The Mayo Clinic describes self-talk as the constant stream of thoughts running through our minds. It further notes that negative self-talk can reinforce pessimism and stress responses, while positive self-talk can improve stress management and resilience.2 This matters for leaders because leadership is often emotional labor disguised as strategy.

Leaders are expected to remain calm under pressure, make difficult decisions, and project confidence even when they are doubting themselves. Under those conditions, what you say and think about yourself becomes critically important.

The Neuroscience Behind Affirmation

Positive affirmation is not about pretending problems don’t exist. Many leaders are often brutally honest about reality. The distinction is that psychologically healthy leaders do not allow negative internal narratives to dominate their thinking. Studies highlighted in positive psychology literature show that positive emotions actually broaden cognitive capacity and improve adaptability.3 Barbara Fredrickson’s broaden-and-build theory demonstrates that positive emotional states help people think more creatively, become more open to new ideas, and strengthen social connection and resilience.4

Neuroscience research also suggests that emotionally intelligent leadership affects the brain activity of others. Positive emotional communication can activate neural pathways associated with openness, receptivity, and collaborative thinking.5 Negative emotional communication, on the other hand, can trigger threat responses and survival-oriented thinking. In simple terms, leaders who consistently operate from panic, cynicism, hostility, or catastrophic thinking often shrink the thinking capacity of everyone around them. Every leader should understand these two things: 1. The brain under threat shrinks; and 2. The brain under encouragement expands.

Neuroscientists now understand that this is not simply metaphorical language. It is biological. Research on fear and threat response suggests that when the brain perceives danger, the amygdala, often described as the brain’s alarm system, rapidly activates and sends signals throughout the brain, essentially communicating, “Pay attention. Something may be wrong.”6

That response is extremely useful if you are avoiding a speeding car or reacting to an immediate physical threat. But leadership often activates the same neurological systems through psychological threats rather than physical ones.

  • An angry email from a parent
  • A hostile board meeting
  • A disappointing evaluation
  • A public mistake
  • Negative comments on social media
  • The fear that you are losing credibility

The brain often responds to those moments as if survival itself is at risk. Under perceived threat, attention narrows. Emotional reactivity increases. Defensive thinking rises. Neuroscientists have found that threatening stimuli activate regions associated with heightened awareness and defensive responses.7 In leadership settings, by extension, this can show up as irritability, micromanaging, or difficulty receiving feedback objectively.

In simple terms, the threatened brain becomes more focused on protection than possibility. That is why language matters so much. When the assistant principal in the workshop saw his struggle as his identity, he was virtually sealing his fate as a failure. That matters enormously because leadership emotions spread.8

Leaders who consistently operate from negativity or defensiveness often shrink the thinking capacity of everyone around them. Leaders who cultivate encouragement often create environments where people feel psychologically safe enough to think clearly and contribute creatively. The emotional climate a leader creates for others often begins with the emotional climate they create within themselves.

item.title: What Does Science Say When “the Science” Refuses to Speak?
item.description:
Politics

What Does Science Say When “the Science” Refuses to Speak?

Scientists have a moral responsibility to be transparent. But not under threat.

Posted August 14, 2026

Key points
  • Faith in scientific integrity has eroded. Forthright testimony is required to repair public trust.
  • Scientists have an ethical responsibility to be transparent, especially in the face of adversity.
  • Scientists should not be compelled to testify under the threat of criminal prosecution or coercion.

In a recent U.S. Senate hearing, Dr. Anthony Fauci refused to answer questions about his scientific views on the COVID-19 pandemic by invoking his Fifth Amendment right against self-incrimination. This is certainly understandable in the current hyper-charged political environment: Dr. Fauci explicitly stated he believed one purpose of the hearing was to legally ensnare him for subsequent criminal charges despite having been granted a broad pardon from President Biden.

From the outset, several key points should be stipulated. First, Dr. Fauci has unique scientific knowledge on the origins of COVID-19, how vaccines were developed and implemented, how treatments were developed and implemented, and on how public health recommendations in response to the pandemic were generated and promulgated. Far from being a chess piece in a partisan political game, this knowledge and testimony is vital for informing and formulating discovery and policy recommendations for the next pandemic and is needed to rebuild public trust in science. Second, although Dr. Fauci has a moral if not legal obligation to present his findings, his testimony should not be coerced or extracted under threat of criminal prosecution. It is also crucial to stipulate that when the pandemic was unfolding, decisions had to be made while utilizing emerging and incomplete data: Imperfect knowledge will sometimes yield incorrect conclusions and recommendations. Indeed, this latter stipulation is precisely needed to ensure that mistakes are minimized in future pandemic response policy.

Dr. Fauci's Questioning and Galileo’s Inquisition

Lessons from another famous episode when a prominent and controversial scientist was compelled to testify may be instructive. As in modern times, the capital city was abuzz with news and opinions regarding an upcoming hearing. But the hearing was in Rome in 1633 and was focused on Galileo Galilei. The questioning body was the Roman Inquisition, and unlike the U.s. Senate, the Inquisition could (and sometimes did) recommend that civil authorities conduct executions and burn people at the stake.

The context of the Galileo hearing was a scientific and religious debate between the geocentric (earth-centered) and heliocentric (sun-centered) models of the solar system. In the early 1600s, Galileo replicated the findings of Nicolaus Copernicus and thereby contradicted the widely accepted centuries-old earth-centered models of venerated scientific geniuses such as Aristotle and Ptolemy. Perhaps worse, this conclusion ran afoul of widely accepted theological teachings, which placed humans as the center of a God-created universe (and solar system). To argue otherwise was viewed as heretical. After testifying, Galileo avoided execution but was sentenced to house arrest for the rest of his life, although only after being compelled to publicly retract his scientific findings.

This tension between scientific integrity and political (and criminal) reality creates a crucial conundrum because one can compellingly argue that the U.S.—and the world—need unencumbered, forthright testimony from the scientist who knows the most about the scientific origins of COVID-19—and the data driving public health decisions made in response to the pandemic. Bear in mind that in previous senate testimony as the pandemic was unfolding, Dr. Fauci was forthcoming, fearless, and at times even confrontational in defending the scientific basis of his decisions in the name of science.

The Dangers of Undermining Science

Indeed, Dr. Fauci explicitly described his guiding philosophy as the most prominent scientist leading the U.S. (and in some ways, the worldwide) response to the COVID-19 pandemic during an interview on “Face the Nation” on Nov. 28, 2021:

But you're talking about systems, you're talking about the CDC, you're talking about the FDA, you're talking about science in general. So, if they want to—I mean, anybody who's looking at this carefully realizes that there's a distinct anti-science flavor to this. So, if they get up and criticize science, nobody's going to know what they're talking about. But if they get up and really aim their bullets at Tony Fauci, well, people could recognize there's a person there. There's a face, there's a voice you can recognize, you see him on television. So, it's easy to criticize, but they're really criticizing science because I represent science. That's dangerous.

The final portion of this quote is worth highlighting:

I'm not going to be around here forever, but science is going to be here forever. And if you damage science, you are doing something very detrimental to society long after I leave. And that's what I worry about.

That is what every scientist past, present, and future should be worried about. It is our responsibility, as scientists, to publicly present our findings, even in the face of adversity. Accepting criticism is part and parcel of what it means to be a scientist. Scientists should rightly anticipate persecution in the arena of ideas and policymaking but not prosecution in a criminal arena.

Controversy and Debate Are Inherent to Scientific Progress

The current passionate scientific—and political—debate over scientific findings and their societal impacts are hardly new. In his book The Demon-Haunted World: Science as a Candle in the Dark, [2] astronomer Carl Sagan provides a masterful and persuasive review of how scientific findings—and scientists—are often controversial and contentious precisely because their theories and discoveries frequently conflict with “conventional wisdom” and popular beliefs.

One could argue that Dr. Fauci has a compelling self-interest to avoid Galileo’s fate of being placed under arrest and should protect himself. On the other hand, he also has a responsibility to publicly explain his findings and decision-making, including when mistakes were made, and answer questions about his recommendations after the threat of coercion is explicitly removed.

Science can only advance when new data and findings, including errors, are dispassionately and objectively reviewed. We can all hope that the authorities and Dr. Fauci (and his attorneys) can reach consensus on terms that no longer result in his “pleading the Fifth” in the face of scrutiny (or dare we say, an inquisition). The current impasse is no doubt “damaging science” and “doing something very damaging to society.” Dr. Fauci does indeed “represent science,” for better and for worse, and should be afforded every opportunity to report his findings in order to illuminate to the U.S. and the world on the inputs and processes utilized during the COVID-19 pandemic response.

item.title: Are You Controlled By Your Partner's Defensiveness?
item.description:
Anger

Are You Controlled By Your Partner's Defensiveness?

To break free from the defensive cycle, you have to first change your response.

Posted August 14, 2026

Nina and her husband Steve were dining at their favorite restaurant. It was particularly loud that night, however, which was irritating for Steve, who had highly sensitive ears. Nonetheless, the conversation was rich and deep, all about the new business project Steve was building. Nina was an engaged listener and curious, not just about the project, but about her husband’s experience, what it was growing and challenging in him. For hours, Nina dove into Steve’s passion and purpose, and the result was an evening of connection and love.

After a few hours, the conversation came to its natural completion, and the couple easily transitioned into silence, holding hands, enjoying their coffee and people-watching.

In that sweet silence, feeling deeply connected, Nina decided to tell Steve about a recent insight she’d had about herself, a discovery that felt important to her on a spiritual level. He responded with a seemingly agitated “I hear you,” but nothing more, which felt odd and out of sync with the mood of the evening.

Nina sat quietly for a few minutes, confused that such a disclosure wouldn’t generate even a single question, and then she mustered the courage to gently tell Steve that she sometimes wished he could be more curious about her, not just about surface things, but about what really mattered to her (like what she’d just shared). Without making any judgments or accusations, she was honest about feeling lonely and shut down when he rejected her invitation to know her more deeply—how his tight “I hear you” with no follow-up left her feeling sad and with a deep longing to be more intimately known and connected.

Nina shared that she craved the same kind of engaged curiosity that she offered him; she also wanted a partner who would stoke the sparks of her passion, help her formulate the unformulated in her, and who could ask questions that would help her know herself better. Still feeling safe and warm, Nina had mustered the courage to be honest about how she was actually feeling and what she really wanted.

In an aggressive tone, Steve said that he didn’t know anything about spiritual matters, so how the hell was he supposed to ask her something about what she’d shared? That wasn’t his field. Despite being frightened by his anger, Nina tried to explain that it wasn’t about understanding the spiritual material; she knew that wasn’t his arena, but rather wanting to know her and what her insight meant in her life.

Her response triggered his rage, and suddenly her husband was shouting at her.

She was always telling him how he needed to be different, to be exactly what she wanted.. He was not going to change for her and was done being told what was wrong with him. She was a control freak and could take him or leave him—as is. If not, he would leave the marriage.

And then he left the restaurant.

Steve slept on the couch that night. The next morning Nina awoke to find him gone, sheets and blankets neatly folded on the arm of the couch and the pillow put away. This was their pattern: Steve raged and then withdrew and sometimes disappeared. He then played the victim who’d been assaulted by her “demands.”

Steve stayed out until dinner time and when he returned, cooked his own meal without a word. Their 16-year-old joined them at the dinner table, and they each spoke with him, but didn’t address each other. He again slept on the couch. The next day, they made a bit of small talk about scheduling; he mentioned that he was going to see a movie they’d talked about seeing together. “I’ll be there for the 6pm show,” he said without directly inviting her. That night Nina didn’t go to the movie but felt overwhelming anxiety, and a kind of terror. Intellectually, she knew that what she’d experienced was unfair, profoundly unkind, and unacceptable. She knew that what she’d said the night before came from a loving place inside her, love for herself and her husband, and was driven by a wish to feel more known, and less lonely—all things she deserved. Still, her nervous system was in code red, which meant that she had to make things right with Steve no matter how unfair or unacceptable it all was.

She spent the evening questioning her timing, the choice to share her feelings at that moment, after such a lovely evening, and in that loud restaurant, knowing how Steve reacted to noise. She wondered why she had such a “relentless” need to feel seen and known. In short, the self-blaming had begun.

By the next morning, Nina had entered the “fawning” stage in their cycle. She was filling the silences with cheerful conversation, complimenting him wherever she could, talking about their summer plans, asking about the film he’d seen; she bought him his favorite cookie, cooked a lovely dinner, and that night, invited him back into their bed and had sex with him.

Her nervous system had kicked into high gear—she instinctively became the “good girl,” the one who behaved and was okay with everything that had happened—that he’d done to her. Terrified by the potential punishment, conflict, abandonment, and all the rest, she tucked her own feelings away and agreed, silently, to be the character in his movie, the perpetrator who’d victimized him with her demands.

After several days of “behaving,” Nina could sense that she’d “won him back.” Steve’s anger relented, and he returned to being her husband, even suggesting that they go to their restaurant for a date night. Without thinking carefully, Nina responded that she didn’t want to risk being with him in a loud place again, essentially, to put herself in harm’s way.

In an instant, Steve was back at full throttle–how dare she accuse him of being the problem. In his diatribe, she’d created a story about him as someone “unsafe” (demonstrated with air quotes), someone who had a “problem” (more air quotes) with noise—who couldn’t control himself. But she was the one out of control; people raised their voices all the time, it didn’t mean anything. What happened the week before was nothing, and she was delusional for thinking it was a big deal. She would never get an apology from him because he did nothing wrong.

They were a long, long way from Nina’s original bid to feel more deeply known; her craving for Steve’s curiosity. Deep down the rabbit hole of accusations, it was clear that Nina’s loneliness, the mention of which had originally set this train in motion, was not going to receive the attention it needed. Blame had bypassed empathy, as it always did.

But then something happened: Nina started shaking, her body went into what felt like a state of shock. All the years of absorbing anger and unkindness, the energy and effort to win him back, the self-abandonment, and the oceans of terror in which she’d been swimming, all of it led her nervous system to finally break. Her body overrode her intellect, and even her primal need for relational security. It spoke for her, without asking, and what came out of her mouth was simply "Stop shouting at me.” Again and again she bellowed it from her gut. And then, as if in a dream, she found herself out on the street. The woman who later walked back into that house, however, was changed.

Sometimes we have to break to change. But we can also address a situation that’s not working before we break. To do that, we have to change our behaviors around anger, and our unconscious participation in the defensive cycle. More to come...
